title: Mission Programming Fundamentals
contentStatus: PROPOSED title/content, pending DiFacto confirmation. Builds on conceptual mission mechanics from L2-M1/L2-M6, going deeper into actual programming. Specific ANT programming interface pending SME confirmation.

sections.title: From Operating Missions to Building Them
learningObjectives: Understand how the Programmer role differs from the Operator role
Recognize the scope of this track relative to L2's mission coverage
sections.content: L2 taught you to assign, monitor, and work with missions that already existed. The Programmer track teaches you to build them - defining new missions, mapping new spaces, and commissioning MoRo for use at new sites. This is a creation and configuration role, not just an operational one.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's Human-Machine Interface (HMI) platform, used for fleet monitoring, mission control, and programming — introduced in L1-M3.

sections.title: Mission Programming Concepts
learningObjectives: Understand the building blocks of a programmed mission
Recognize how waypoints and conditions combine into a complete mission
sections.content: A programmed mission is built from waypoints (specific locations on the map) connected by a defined sequence, optionally combined with conditional logic (covered conceptually in L2-M6) for more complex behavior. Programming a mission means defining this structure explicitly, rather than working with missions someone else has already built.

keyTerms.note: A specific, defined location on MoRo's map used as a reference point within a programmed mission.

sections.title: Setting Waypoints
learningObjectives: Understand the general process of defining a waypoint
Recognize considerations for reliable waypoint placement
sections.content: Setting a waypoint means marking a specific location on MoRo's map as a reference point a mission can use - a pickup station, a drop point, a staging area. Reliable waypoint placement considers factors like reachability (can MoRo actually navigate to and stop precisely at this location) and clearance (is there enough space for the operation intended at that point). Exact waypoint-setting procedure within ANT will be confirmed against the live system.

sections.title: Sequencing a Mission
learningObjectives: Understand how waypoints are combined into a sequenced mission
Recognize the difference between a simple linear sequence and a more complex structure
sections.content: The simplest mission structure is linear - visit waypoints in a fixed order. More complex missions may involve conditional branching (introduced conceptually in L2-M6) or repeating loops. Programming starts with getting the linear case right and reliable before introducing additional complexity.

sections.title: Testing a Programmed Mission
learningObjectives: Apply the mission validation principle from L2-M1 to newly programmed missions
Understand what additional scrutiny a newly programmed mission needs compared to a pre-existing one
sections.content: Testing a newly programmed mission carries more uncertainty than testing a minor modification to an existing one, since nothing about the mission's behavior has been validated yet. Programmers should expect to iterate - testing, identifying issues, adjusting waypoints or sequencing, and retesting - before a new mission is considered reliable enough for routine operational use.

sections.title: Documenting a Programmed Mission
learningObjectives: Understand what documentation a programmed mission requires
Recognize why this matters for future maintenance or modification
sections.content: A programmed mission should be documented with its intended purpose, waypoint logic, and any conditional behavior - not just left as a working but unexplained configuration. This matters because missions get modified over time, and whoever modifies it later (possibly not the original programmer) needs to understand the original intent to avoid breaking it.

questions.question: How does the Programmer role differ from the Operator role covered at L2?
options: Programmers build and configure missions, rather than just operating existing ones
Programmers only work with hardware, never software
questions.feedback: Correct. The Programmer track is a creation/configuration role, building on L2's operational foundation.

questions.question: What is a waypoint?
options: A specific, defined location on MoRo's map used as a reference point in a mission
questions.feedback: Correct. Waypoints are the basic location-based building blocks of a programmed mission.

questions.question: What should be considered when placing a waypoint?
options: Nothing - any location works equally well
Reachability and clearance for the intended operation at that point
Only the distance from the charging dock
questions.feedback: Correct. Reliable waypoint placement accounts for whether MoRo can actually navigate to and operate at that location.

questions.question: What structure should mission programming start with before adding complexity?
options: Programming should start with the most complex case
questions.feedback: Correct. Getting the simple linear case right first is the recommended starting point.

questions.question: Why does a newly programmed mission need more testing scrutiny than a minor modification?
options: It doesn't - both need the same level of testing
Nothing about a new mission's behavior has been validated yet
New missions are always simpler and need less testing
questions.feedback: Correct. A newly programmed mission carries more uncertainty, requiring more thorough validation.
